extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers interested in moral/philosophical essays, education, and conduct
extracted.subtask_short: literary essay on education and friendship
extracted.subtask_description: A Renaissance-era personal essay (Montaigne) discussing standards and practical guidance for education, language learning, theatre, belief, and the nature of friendship. It mixes autobiographical example with prescriptive observations about how to teach, how to judge truth, and what constitutes friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value concise, fertile thought over ornate eloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato: Athenians study fulness and elegancy of speaking; Lacedaemonians affect brevity; those of Crete aim more at the fecundity of conception than the fertility of speech; and these are the best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between mere ornament (words, elocution) and substantive thought; praises brevity and fecundity of idea over fine speaking. Warns against spending life only in eloquence and urges understanding one's own and neighbours' language for practical conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer practical comprehension of one's language to affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘I would first understand my own language, and that of my neighbours, with whom most of my business and conversation lies.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admonishes against affecting rare or foreign words; stresses usefulness of knowing and speaking the language used in ordinary life rather than pursuing empty verbal ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language education by early immersion (household-language method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne's father employed a German tutor and household members who spoke only Latin to the child so that by six he spoke as pure Latin as the master himself, 'without art, book, grammar, or precept.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete method: surrounding the child with native/target-language speakers; give child themes in bad Latin to translate into good Latin; use games for declensions. Example shows rapid, natural acquisition and spillover into household and village usage. Also warns that discontinuance and later college practices can corrupt initial gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educate by liberty and delight; avoid severity and constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Father's rule: make the child relish science and duty 'by an unforced will, and of my own voluntary motion, and to educate my soul in all liberty and delight, without any severity or constraint.' He awakened the child gently with music rather than violent rousing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer playful, pleasant, and voluntary methods (games, music, gentle encouragement) to coercion, whipping, or harsh discipline. The aim is to foster appetite for learning rather than fear or rote compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor education to the child's temperament; avoid universal prescriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne notes his own 'heavy, idle, and indisposed' nature and slow wit; he calls the child's mind 'sterile and improper soil' for certain methods and criticises blindly following the common methods of the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize individual differences (disposition, memory, temperament); avoid forcing standard remedies or length of instruction that don't fit the child. One-size-fits-all college systems can undo early gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow and cultivate natural reading interests to build appetite for learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne's first taste for books came from Ovid's Metamorphoses; his tutor discreetly allowed this diversion which whetted his appetite and enabled him to read Virgil, Terence, Plautus, and comedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than forbidding a child's preferred reading, discreetly permit and harness it to stimulate broader learning. Suppressing early pleasures in reading risks producing hatred of books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allure appetite and affections; avoid teaching by lash and rote
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘There is nothing like alluring the appetite and affections; otherwise you make nothing but so many asses laden with books; by dint of the lash, you give them their pocketful of learning to keep.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective teaching seeks to engage desire and affection for the subject so that knowledge is embraced and internalized rather than merely stored by force. Rote memorisation without appetite yields useless knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use theatre and acting as proper educational exercises for youth
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne defends young persons of condition playing parts in Latin tragedies and praises acting as an exercise for assurance of countenance, voice, and gesture. He cites Greek practice and thinks well-governed cities should provide spectacles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acting develops practical personal faculties (presence, speech, gesture) and public theatres can serve civic and social ends. Opposing such entertainments is unjust; they augment society and friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not measure truth and error by the limits of your own capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘To condemn them as impossible, is by a temerarious presumption to pretend to know the utmost bounds of possibility.’ Montaigne warns against arrogantly rejecting phenomena because they exceed personal understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt intellectual humility: distinguish the impossible from the unusual; avoid condemning reports or phenomena as false merely because they seem incredible. Leave uncertain matters in suspense rather than dismissing them outright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspend judgment when credible testimony reports unusual phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne cites authorities (Plutarch, Pliny, St. Augustine) who report marvels and miracles and argues that offhand condemnation of such reports is 'a singular impudence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give due respect to testimony from reputable sources; rather than instantaneous disbelief, treat unusual reports with caution and openness—unless there is clear reason to reject them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid selective theological concessions; either fully submit or reject ecclesiastical authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne criticises Catholics who 'grant to their opponents some of the articles in question' as appearing moderate but actually yielding ground and arming the adversary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On matters of ecclesiastical polity and obedience, partial concessions can be dangerous. One should recognise the implications of conceding particular points rather than casually treating them as indifferent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship is voluntary, spiritual, and distinct from natural or utilitarian ties
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship is not the same as children's respect for parents, nor the fraternal tie, nor marriage; it is 'voluntary liberty' producing 'affection and friendship' and is nourished by communication and likeness of manners and inclinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A true and perfect friendship requires free choice, equality of mind, mutual counsel, steady communication, and absence of mixed motives (profit, social obligation). Natural relations imposed by law or blood rarely constitute full friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship grows by enjoyment; love is fleeting and physical
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne contrasts friendship and erotic love: love is 'more active, more eager, and more sharp' but 'precipitant, fickle, moving, and inconstant' and is destroyed by fruition; friendship 'only grows up, is nourished and improved by enjoyment' and is spiritual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the differing natures: do not conflate carnal love (which thrives on pursuit and novelty) with true friendship (which strengthens through shared enjoyment and soul-level communion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural family ties often lack the equality and freedom required for true friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Parental, filial, and fraternal relations are often asymmetrical (duties, inheritance, disparity of age), and thus cannot readily support the mutual freedom and communication friendship needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious in expecting parental/filial/brotherly relationships to fulfill the same role as voluntary friendship; social or legal bonds can impede the frankness and equal counsel friendship requires.
